The entry lacks three older facts: the same kind of tool is now in registered human trials aimed at a person's own genes, including the cholesterol gene PCSK9 (the STX-1150 trial, registry entry NCT07428473, started 2026-06-30), a muscle-disease gene (the EPI-321 trial, NCT06907875, with a company release of 2026-06-26 on six-month results) and a second hepatitis B trial (CRMA-1001, NCT07200193). The description's line that the human trial is aimed at a virus 'rather than an ageing gene' is therefore out of date as a picture of the field.

Peer-reviewed paper in Cell Stem Cell (Ye and colleagues, published online 2026-11-05): epigenome editors silenced a platelet gene in human blood-forming stem cells in the laboratory, and the silencing held for four months after the cells were transplanted into mice. Tune Therapeutics' news page lists an item dated 2026-11-05 saying its editing platform was named gene editing platform of the year in an industry awards scheme; the page lists no new clinical data, publication or phase 2 start since the release of 2026-05-30. records.found: No peer-reviewed report dated 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-09 shows a clock reading falling after a treatment, and the follow-up trial TRIIM-X (NCT04375657) is unchanged on the registry since 2025-05-07, still 'recruiting' with a completion date of 2025-12 that has passed and no results. One thing in the window bears on the test without meeting it: a placebo-controlled trial first posted on 2026-11-03 (NCT07912164) makes a fall of at least 5 per cent on a named DNA-marks clock (DunedinPACE) one of the two ways a participant counts as a responder on its main measure.

findings.what: Registry entry NCT07912164, first posted 2026-11-03: a randomised, placebo-controlled, quadruple-masked trial by the company Human Biome S.A. of gut-microbe transplant capsules in an estimated 68 adults aged 45 to 80, not yet recruiting, start estimated 2026-12, primary completion estimated 2027-12. Its main measure is a responder rate, where a responder has either a fall of at least 5 per cent on the DunedinPACE pace-of-ageing clock or a fall of at least 25 per cent in an inflammation marker. A registration only; no result.

Registry entry NCT07906041, first posted 2026-10-30 and updated 2026-11-02: a phase 2, randomised, unmasked trial of tirzepatide in an estimated 22 people, sponsored by the Atria Research and Global Health Institute, whose main measure is the change in a brain-age reading taken from blood proteins at six months. The clock is read from proteins, not from the marks on DNA, so it sits beside this entry's test and not inside it.

Registry entry for TRIIM-X (NCT04375657) read on 2026-11-09: recruiting, status last verified 2025-05, last updated 2025-05-07, primary completion 2025-12, 85 people estimated, no results posted. Same as the record's reading of 2026-10-17.

A Nature Biotechnology paper applying six blood-protein clocks to a 12-week trial of the drug rentosertib was covered by Fight Aging! on 2026-11-09; the paper itself is dated 2026-09-07 and is already in the records' publications log.

Peer-reviewed paper in Aging Cell (Borrus and colleagues, 2026-10-01), outside the window and not in the records: when earlier single-clock treatment studies were re-run with more clocks, no further clock reached significance; the authors propose three checks before a clock result is trusted (reliable clocks respond, mortality-trained or pace clocks respond, several clocks move the same way) and say some published single-clock findings may need re-examining. It bears on what 'a validated clock' should mean in this entry's test; the 2019 trial reported four clocks moving together.

findings.what: Peer-reviewed recommendations in the Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore (Chen and colleagues, 2026-11-04): lecanemab is approved in Singapore and a local expert group sets out who should receive it and how they should be monitored, with a call for a national registry. Shows the drug entering practice in another country; gives no count of people treated.

records.found: The week's records point towards wider use, which supports the early end of the wide-use range, but none gives the share of eligible patients treated, so the test is not met. Pfizer's results of 2026-11-03 put sales of the tafamidis family at $1,773 million for the quarter, up from $1,591 million, on 'continued market expansion' in the United States; Alnylam's release of 2026-11-09 reports five-year results for the rival drug vutrisiran and says more than 14,000 patients worldwide have been treated with it; and a peer-reviewed four-year follow-up of the same trial appeared in Circulation on 2026-11-03. Against that, the entry lacks an older result that counts the other way: a late-stage trial of another rival, eplontersen, in 1,432 people did not meet its main measure (presented and published 2026-08-28), which weakens the estimate's reasoning that arriving competitors will widen use.

findings.what: Pfizer's third-quarter 2026 results release, filed with the United States securities regulator on 2026-11-03: revenue of the tafamidis family (sold as Vyndaqel, Vyndamax and Vynmac) was $1,773 million for the quarter against $1,591 million a year earlier (United States $1,086 million, elsewhere $687 million), up 12 per cent before currency effects, which the company puts down mainly to continued market expansion in the United States and more diagnosis abroad. Revenue only; no count of patients or share of those eligible.

Alnylam release of 2026-11-09, data presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026: five-year follow-up of the HELIOS-B trial of vutrisiran (a drug that stops the liver making the protein), comparing people on it from the start with those who began after the placebo period; the combined risk of death and repeat heart events was 41 per cent lower in all 654 people and 48 per cent lower in the 395 not on tafamidis at the start. The release says the p-values are nominal, names no journal paper, and says more than 14,000 patients worldwide have been treated with the drug.

Peer-reviewed paper in Circulation (Garcia-Pavia and colleagues, online 2026-11-03): one-year results of the open-label extension of HELIOS-B, through month 48. Of 654 people in the trial, 466 entered the extension; those on vutrisiran throughout had a 37 per cent lower risk of death from any cause than those who started on placebo (hazard ratio 0.63). A peer-reviewed report that a drug of this kind lowers deaths, which the test already counts as met; it adds weight, not a stage.

Peer-reviewed paper in Clinical Research in Cardiology (Morbach and colleagues, 2026-11-02): early routine use of the second stabiliser, acoramidis, in Germany. A prescription database covering 82 per cent of reimbursed prescriptions found 289 people given it between April and September 2025; median age 82; 86 per cent had not had tafamidis before. A published uptake count for one drug in one country, with no figure for those eligible.

Intellia's third-quarter 2026 results release (2026-11-05, read in the copy filed with the securities regulator): enrolment in the late-stage trial of its one-dose gene editor nexiguran ziclumeran in the nerve form of the disease was completed in the third quarter, past its target of 60; the heart-disease trial (MAGNITUDE) is still enrolling, with no numbers or data date given; doctors are now given the immune-gene test results for people in both trials. The registry entry for MAGNITUDE (NCT06128629) was updated on 2026-11-04 and still reads recruiting, 1,200 people, primary completion 2027-12.

Alnylam filing of 2026-11-05 with the securities regulator: the board authorised buying back up to $1.0 billion of shares on 2026-11-02, and the company's head of commercialisation will leave in December 2026. Nothing on the drug, its trials or its use.

Not in the records: the CARDIO-TTRansform trial of eplontersen (another drug that stops the liver making the protein; Ionis and AstraZeneca) in 1,432 people with the heart disease showed no significant difference from placebo in deaths from heart causes and repeat heart events over up to 140 weeks; presented at the European Society of Cardiology congress and published in the New England Journal of Medicine the same day, as reported by the American College of Cardiology on 2026-08-28. Most participants (57 per cent) were already on a stabiliser, and those were the ones with no clear gain. The journal paper itself was not opened.

BridgeBio's third-quarter 2026 results release (2026-10-29, read in the filed copy): United States revenue of acoramidis was $253.2 million for the quarter, about $145 million more than a year earlier; the drug is approved in the United States, the European Union, Japan, Switzerland, Brazil, the United Kingdom and Australia. No patient count. Outside the window and not in the records.

Registry updates in the window with no change of substance: the HELIOS-B entry (NCT04153149, updated 2026-11-02, active, results first posted 2025-10-21) and AstraZeneca's eplontersen trial in Chinese patients (NCT06194825, updated 2026-11-06, active, primary completion 2026-05-13, no results posted).

records.story_why: Five-year survival data for a second kind of drug against this protein, a peer-reviewed four-year report, and the first drug still growing at about $7 billion a year make a short post on how far this treatment has spread; the post should also carry the August failure of eplontersen, which the site has not yet recorded. The wide-use years: the growth and the 14,000-patient count argue that 2027 to 2030 is reasonable, while the absence of any published share of eligible patients, and one competitor's failure, argue against moving them earlier.

records.found: Nothing dated 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-09 bears on this record: no peer-reviewed report of a measured reversal in a person, no registry change to the eye trial (NCT07290244, last updated 2026-05-19) and no regulator's decision. A laboratory paper on delivering the resetting genes as circular RNA was covered by a news site on 2026-11-03 but was published on 2026-07-26 and is cell work in a dish.

findings.what: Peer-reviewed paper in Stem Cell Research & Therapy (Luo and colleagues, published 2026-07-26; covered by Fight Aging! on 2026-11-03): three resetting genes delivered as circular RNA reduced signs of ageing in laboratory-grown human stem cells without turning them into embryonic-like cells. Dish work, outside the window, and not an animal or a person.

Peer-reviewed paper in the journal Aging (Meiners and colleagues, 2026-10-27), outside the window and not in the records: a re-analysis of gene-activity data from the liver, kidney and spleen of old mice given seven months of partial resetting found age-related inflammation signals turned down in liver and kidney, and in the spleen signs of raised cell division that the authors flag as a possible risk; they call for larger controlled studies. A re-analysis of existing animal data, with a caution attached; it changes no stage.

unmatched.what: The trial registry posted results on 2026-11-05 for Janssen's phase 2 trial of posdinemab, an antibody against tau (the other protein that builds up in Alzheimer's disease), in 523 people with early disease (NCT04619420). The entry lists the trial as terminated, with the reason given as the drug not reaching statistical significance in slowing clinical decline.
unmatched.why_it_matters: A result that counts against: an antibody against a second age-related brain protein failed in a sizeable controlled trial, and the site's broken-proteins branch has no entry that would carry it.

unmatched.what: Intellia's third-quarter release of 2026-11-05 says the United States regulator accepted its licence application for lonvo-z, a one-dose gene editor given inside the body for hereditary angioedema, in September 2026 with priority review and a target decision date of 2027-03-10, with no advisory committee currently planned; the company plans a launch in the first quarter of 2027.
unmatched.why_it_matters: It dates the first possible approval of an in-body gene editor, which belongs to the site's entry on a gene edited inside a person's body (not in this packet); the records hold only the earlier expectation that the application would be accepted in the second half of 2026.

unmatched.what: Peer-reviewed randomised, double-blind, controlled trial in European Heart Journal Open (Piercy and colleagues, 2026-11-04): 61 apparently healthy adults were given a multi-ingredient supplement powder sold for ageing or a control for six months; 43 completed. Against control, the widening of an arm artery in response to blood flow (the main measure) improved by 2.9 percentage points, the speed of the pulse wave (a measure of arterial stiffness) fell by 1.18 metres a second and systolic blood pressure fell by 6.1 mmHg. Coverage on lifespan.io (2026-11-06) says the maker supplied the product and helped fund the study, and that about a third of participants were lost to follow-up.
unmatched.why_it_matters: A small controlled trial reporting less stiff arteries in healthy adults from a product sold as an ageing treatment. It fits none of this packet's tests (it is not a cross-link breaker and names no recycling mechanism), and it is maker-funded with heavy drop-out, but readers will meet it.

unmatched.what: Peer-reviewed mouse study in Cell Reports (Zhang and colleagues, 2026-11-04): a protein deposit made of antibody light chains builds up around liver blood vessels with age, and clearing it with the antibody anselamimab restored the aged liver's ability to regrow after part of it was removed.
unmatched.why_it_matters: An animal result in which clearing an age-related protein deposit restores a lost function, using an antibody already tested in people for another disease; it is a different protein from any on the site's broken-proteins branch.

unmatched.what: Registry entry NCT07906041 (first posted 2026-10-30, updated 2026-11-02): a small phase 2 trial of the weight-loss drug tirzepatide whose main measure is a brain-age reading taken from blood proteins at six months; 22 people, sponsored by the Atria Research and Global Health Institute.
unmatched.why_it_matters: A trial of an approved drug with an ageing clock as its main measure, which belongs with the site's entry on a treatment slowing a clock in a controlled trial (not in this packet). Also listed under the biological-age record.

unmatched.what: An editorial on lifespan.io dated 2026-11-05 says senior officials of the United States regulator named longevity a priority at a Boston research conference in October 2026 and spoke of fit-for-purpose measures and development routes, without declaring ageing a disease. The underlying report was not opened and the editorial gives no date for the remarks.
unmatched.why_it_matters: Regulatory acceptance of ageing measures sets the pace for several clinic-rung estimates on the site; this is second-hand and undated, so it is a lead to check, not a fact to enter.
